title: CSS Reset & Normalize
summary: Browsers add default styles, so a reset helps a project begin from consistent rules.

subtopics.title: Main property
subtopics.explanation: A user-agent stylesheet is the browser’s built-in set of styles. It supplies defaults for margins, fonts, buttons, and display behavior. These defaults help a page work before custom CSS, but some details vary across browsers. Inspect the defaults before deciding that they are a problem to solve. Default rules provide useful behavior as well as appearance. Compare the built-in style with the design requirement before removing it. Browser defaults are like a starter template supplied with a new notebook.

subtopics.title: What it changes
subtopics.explanation: A reset removes or changes browser defaults to create a consistent starting point. It can also remove useful spacing or focus appearance. Treat it like clearing a workbench: keep the tools the project needs. Read the reset rules and restore meaningful focus indicators and control behavior. A reset should be small enough to understand. When a control loses a visible state, restore it deliberately instead of adding a broad override.

subtopics.title: Another useful choice
subtopics.explanation: A normalize stylesheet aims to make useful defaults behave more consistently across browsers. It is like adjusting an uneven table rather than removing it. It may suit a project that wants semantic defaults with fewer surprises. Know what it adds before installing another dependency. Normalize files address selected browser differences; they do not guarantee identical rendering. Test supported browsers for the parts of the interface that matter.

subtopics.title: Common behavior
subtopics.explanation: `box-sizing: border-box` makes a declared width include padding and border. This makes sizing easier to predict. Apply it consistently, including pseudo-elements when needed. A reset can establish this baseline, but the team should understand the rule rather than copy it without context. Border-box makes declared dimensions include padding and border, which reduces arithmetic. It does not decide the layout width or prevent content overflow. Border-box is like measuring the outside of a packed box, not only its contents.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: Keep keyboard focus indicators visible. Removing outlines without a replacement makes it hard to see which control is active. Test the baseline with keyboard-only use and restore a clear focus style. A reset should simplify later styling without making the interface harder to operate. Keyboard focus is an interaction state. Make its outline clear against adjacent colors and verify it remains visible in each theme. A focus outline is like a visible marker showing which control is currently selected.

foundations.overview: Browsers include default styles for headings, lists, buttons, and other elements. These defaults vary, so a reset or normalize stylesheet creates a consistent starting point. Think of it like leveling a workbench before building. Use a small, understood baseline rather than copying a large file blindly, and preserve focus outlines and useful native behavior.
foundations.whyItMatters: A baseline can reduce cross-browser surprises, but broad resets can remove useful defaults. Keep only rules the team understands and verifies.
foundations.browserPerspective: The UA stylesheet is the lowest layer of the cascade; your reset overrides it with author styles. Because UA rules have the lowest origin priority, even low-specificity author selectors in your reset win, which is why a simple body { margin: 0 } reliably removes the default.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Nearly every project loads a reset or normalize first — bundled by frameworks (Bootstrap's Reboot, Tailwind's Preflight) or hand-rolled as a small custom reset at the top of the stylesheet.
foundations.businessImpact: Consistent cross-browser rendering reduces QA churn and visual bugs, getting features shipped faster with fewer support complaints about 'it looks wrong in Safari'.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A predictable baseline (especially border-box) makes layout math intuitive and prevents a long tail of spacing and sizing bugs, saving debugging time across the team.
foundations.performanceImpact: Resets are tiny and add negligible cost; a minimal modern reset is a few hundred bytes versus the larger full Normalize.css, so prefer the smaller one when you don't need every fix.
commonUseCases: Removing the default body margin and block-element margins
Establishing a base font, line-height, and consistent form-control fonts
Start a new app with consistent box sizing.
Preserve native controls while applying a deliberate design system.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A reset and Normalize.css are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A hard reset strips defaults to zero; Normalize.css preserves useful defaults and only fixes inconsistencies.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You don't need a reset because browsers are consistent now.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Defaults still differ (body margin, form controls, list styling), and border-box alone is worth applying everywhere.

commonMisconceptions.myth: box-sizing: border-box changes how big the element looks by default.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It changes what width/height measure (including padding/border), making sizing predictable, not arbitrarily resizing things.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A reset removes every browser difference.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A reset can normalize selected properties but does not make all browsers identical.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Removing all defaults creates a neutral page.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It can remove useful semantics in appearance and keyboard focus unless those styles are restored.

visualExplorer.title: From browser defaults to a clean baseline
visualExplorer.caption: Step through what a reset removes and standardizes before your own styles apply.

steps.title: Raw HTML + UA styles
steps.description: The browser's User-Agent stylesheet adds body margin, heading margins, list bullets, and default fonts — and these differ between browsers.

steps.title: Apply border-box
steps.description: box-sizing: border-box on all elements makes width include padding and border, so sizing math is intuitive.

steps.title: Remove margins
steps.description: Zeroing the body margin and default block margins removes surprise gaps and margin-collapse issues.

steps.title: Set sensible defaults
steps.description: A base font, comfortable line-height, and responsive images give a pleasant, consistent starting point.

steps.title: Your styles on top
steps.description: With a predictable baseline, your design styles behave the same across browsers.

codeLab.title: Write a modern minimal reset
codeLab.instructions: Build a small reset in the empty reset section: apply box-sizing: border-box to all elements and pseudo-elements, remove default margins, give the body a comfortable line-height, and make images responsive. Hint: target *, *::before, *::after for box-sizing, and img for max-width.

keyTakeaways: A user-agent stylesheet is the browser’s built-in set of styles.
A reset removes or changes browser defaults to create a consistent starting point.
A normalize stylesheet aims to make useful defaults behave more consistently across browsers.
`box-sizing: border-box` makes a declared width include padding and border.
